# Repeat: null distributions and the thousand-test trap {#sec-repeat}

## The problem

Your methylation collaborator is back, and the project has grown up. She now has **1,200 CpG
sites** measured in **30 tumor samples and 30 normal samples** — at every site, in every sample,
a read count and a methylated fraction, exactly the measurement you built in
@sec-simulating-a-process. She wants the sites where tumor and normal genuinely differ, because
the top of that list gets validated by pyrosequencing at real cost per site.

She has already looked, and the differences are *everywhere*: almost no site shows exactly the
same fraction in both groups. Of course it doesn't — you spent last chapter measuring the wobble
in any finite sample. Two groups of thirty will differ at every site by sampling variability
alone, at a site where the biology is identical.

So the real question is not "which sites differ" — all of them do. It is: **which differences are
larger than the wobble two identical groups would show — and when you ask that question 1,200
times, what happens to the answers?**

The second half is where this chapter earns its title. The answer to the first half is a tool;
the answer to the second is a warning label that most working scientists learned the hard way.

## The story

This week's operation is **repeat**, and it composes what you already own. One site is last
chapter's story twice: tumor's true fraction $m$, normal's true fraction $m$ — *the same $m$,
because we are building the world where nothing is going on* — each observed through finite
reads in finite samples. The whole experiment is that story repeated 1,200 times, one $m$ per
site, spread across the genome's range.

The world where nothing is going on has a name — the **null world** — and building it explicitly
is the move of the week. It answers a question no amount of staring at her real data can: *what
do purely accidental differences look like, at this depth, with these group sizes, across this
many sites?* Whatever that world produces, her data must beat.

## The story, as code

One site's group difference, then 1,200 of them. The inner function is @sec-simulating-a-process
compressed to its built-in form.

```{python}
import numpy as np

def group_fraction(m, n_samples, n_reads, rng):
    """Average observed methylation across one group's samples."""
    return rng.binomial(n_reads, m, n_samples).mean() / n_reads

def null_scan(site_truths, n_samples, n_reads, rng):
    """Observed tumor-minus-normal difference at every site, when NO site truly differs."""
    return np.array([group_fraction(m, n_samples, n_reads, rng)
                     - group_fraction(m, n_samples, n_reads, rng)
                     for m in site_truths])

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
truths = rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 1200)        # each site its own methylation level...
diffs = null_scan(truths, 30, 25, rng)      # ...identical in both groups
print(f"largest difference in a world with nothing in it: {np.abs(diffs).max():.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "1,200 tumor-minus-normal differences from a world where no site differs. None of this is biology."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.hist(diffs, bins=40, color="#2a78d6")
ax.set_xlabel("observed difference in methylation fraction (tumor − normal)")
ax.set_ylabel("sites")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

Sit with that histogram for a moment. Every one of those differences was produced by *nothing*.
Some sites in the nothing-world differ by a full eight points of methylation — differences a
reasonable person would call "clearly higher in tumor" if they met them one at a time.

## Playing with the story

Pick one site and make the question precise. Say its observed difference is 0.045. Is that
surprising? You have the machine that answers it: run *that site's* null world many times and
count how often nothing-at-all produces a difference at least that big — in either direction,
since a difference of −0.045 is exactly as extreme as +0.045.

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m, observed = 0.5, 0.045
null = np.array([group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
                 for _ in range(2000)])
p = (np.abs(null) >= abs(observed)).mean()
print(f"nothing produces a difference ≥ {observed} about {p:.1%} of the time")
```

That fraction is the **p-value** — nothing more exotic than *how often the null world beats your
observation*. Around 8% here: mildly unusual, the kind of thing nothing-at-all does a few times
in every hundred tries. **Predict before running:** if you compute this for *all 1,200 sites of
the null world* and histogram the p-values, what shape must appear? Not roughly — exactly. Think
about what a p-value of 0.30 means, and how often the null world should produce something its own
top 30% beats.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "P-values for 1,200 sites where nothing is going on. Flat is what honesty looks like."
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
pvals = np.empty(1200)
for i, m in enumerate(truths):
    obs = group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
    null = np.array([group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
                     for _ in range(300)])
    pvals[i] = (np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.hist(pvals, bins=20, color="#2a78d6")
ax.axhline(60, color="#52514e", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("p-value")
ax.set_ylabel("sites")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
print(f"sites with p < 0.05: {(pvals < 0.05).sum()} of 1200")
```

Flat — by construction, not coincidence: a p-value of 0.05 means "the null beats this 5% of the
time," so under the null, 5% of p-values land below 0.05, 10% below 0.10, and so on. Which
delivers the number that should worry you: in a scan with *nothing to find*, at the conventional
p < 0.05, **dozens of sites come up "significant"** — 54 in the run above, against the
$1200 \times 0.05 = 60$ the arithmetic promises. Not because anything is wrong with the
test. Because you asked an honest 1-in-20 question 1,200 times.

## Where the numbers come from

Now build her actual situation: a world that is *mostly* nothing plus a little something — 60
sites where tumor truly runs 0.07 higher, hidden among 1,140 where nothing happens. You know
which is which, because you built it. Run the identical analysis and grade the discovery list:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The discovery list, graded against the truth only the simulator knows."
rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
base = rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 1200)
n_true, delta = 60, 0.07                     # sites 0..59 truly differ
pvals = np.empty(1200)
for i, m in enumerate(base):
    m_tumor = m + (delta if i < n_true else 0.0)
    obs = group_fraction(m_tumor, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
    null = np.array([group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
                     for _ in range(300)])
    pvals[i] = (np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)).mean()

hits = pvals < 0.05
real, false = hits[:n_true].sum(), hits[n_true:].sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
ax.barh(["false discoveries", "real discoveries"], [false, real],
        color=["#eb6834", "#2a78d6"])
for y, v in enumerate([false, real]):
    ax.text(v + 1.5, y, str(v), va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("sites reported at p < 0.05")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
print(f"list: {hits.sum()} sites — {real} real, {false} false — {false/hits.sum():.0%} of the list is noise")
```

Read the composition, because it is the whole chapter: the scan found most of the real sites —
and **almost half the list is false** — the accidents the flat histogram promised, right on
schedule.
Nothing was dishonest. Every p-value did precisely what it claims. The list is still half noise,
because *real effects were rare and questions were plentiful* — 60 truths cannot outnumber the
accidents that 1,140 nothings generate at 1-in-20.

That ratio — how much of the reported list is noise — is the number her pyrosequencing budget
actually cares about, and notice what it depends on: not just the threshold, but **how rare true
effects are**, which nobody knows in advance. Tighten the threshold to p < 0.01 and the accidents
drop toward eleven while most real sites survive; every choice trades real discoveries kept
against false ones admitted, and defending that trade is part of reporting the list.

## The notation

Two compressions this week, both small. The p-value, said precisely:

> *the p-value is the probability that the null world produces a result at least as extreme as
> the one observed.*

Every word is load-bearing — *null world* (a model you built, of nothing happening), *at least as
extreme* (both directions, unless you can justify otherwise before looking), *produces* (you can
always get it by running the world, which is how you got every one above).

And the accounting rule you watched happen:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{false positives}] = m_{\text{null}} \cdot \alpha
$$

The expected number of accidental discoveries is the number of truly-null questions times the
threshold. You cannot know $m_{\text{null}}$ — but $m_{\text{null}} \le$ the number of tests, so
$1200 \times 0.05 = 60$ is the ceiling on accidents, known *before any data arrives*. A scan's
list should always be read next to that number.

## A worked design

The weekly full pass on an adjacent problem — Frame, Decompose, Select, Anticipate.

> **The problem.** A water authority screens **200 wells** monthly for arsenic exceedance.
> The assay is noisy, so each well's monthly result is a measurement, not a verdict. This month
> **9 wells exceeded** the threshold; last month it was 6; the month before, 7. Remediation means
> excavating a well at significant cost, and false alarms burn community trust. The board asks:
> **is contamination spreading, and which specific wells should we dig up?**

**Frame.** Two questions wearing one sentence, and they need different machinery. "Is it
spreading" is about the *count* — is 9-of-200 surprising given assay noise and each well's
history? "Which wells" is 200 *individual* questions asked simultaneously — this month's
scan is a 200-test experiment, and some exceedances are the assay's 1-in-whatever accidents.
I am treating wells as independent for the count question, and flagging now that they are not —
wells share aquifers, and neighboring wells' results move together, which makes clusters of
exceedance both more suspicious as contamination and more producible by shared noise.

**Decompose.** (1) From each well's history, a null world: assay noise around that well's
ordinary level. (2) The count question: simulate 200 wells' ordinary months, count exceedances,
locate 9 in that distribution. (3) The which-wells question: per-well p-values, read against the
expected number of accidents — with 200 wells at a 3% accident rate, six exceedances is the
*baseline*, not a signal. (4) A decision rule that prices the asymmetry: digging up a clean well
costs money; missing a contaminated one costs health — the threshold is not 0.05 by reflex.

**Select.** The method must produce per-well evidence *and* the scan-wide accident count, and it
must let the board move the threshold and watch both costs respond — a fixed verdict is worth
less than the dial. Forward simulation from each well's own history does this. The alternative
I am not taking is flagging wells above a fixed concentration cutoff, which I concede is simpler
and auditable; it fails because wells differ in baseline and in assay noise, so one cutoff is
strict for clean wells and blind for dirty ones.

**Anticipate.** How could my answer be wrong, and how would I know? First: each well's "ordinary
level" comes from its own history — if a well has been quietly contaminated all along, its
history *is* the contamination, my null learns it, and the well becomes invisible; I would check
wells whose baseline sits near the health limit by absolute standard, not just by surprise.
Second: the aquifer correlation I set aside — a shared-noise month produces a cluster that my
independent-wells count question over-reads as spreading; before alarming the board I would ask
whether this month's 9 share a water table. Third: 9 versus 6 versus 7 is three months of a
count whose ordinary wobble I have not yet measured — the trend question may simply be
unanswerable this early, and saying so is a finding.

## When the model is wrong

Box's warning from @sec-simulating-a-process applies with a twist this week: the null world *is
a model* — the most important one you built — and everything the scan concluded assumed it was
the right model of "nothing going on." Three ways that can fail.

**Choosing the direction after seeing the data nearly doubles the accident rate.** The
"at least as extreme in either direction" clause is not pedantry. Suppose an analyst computes a
one-directional p-value — but picks the direction *after looking at which way the difference
went*. Every test is still individually defensible-looking. Watch the accident rate:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
flagged = 0
for _ in range(2000):
    obs = group_fraction(0.5, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(0.5, 30, 25, rng)
    null = np.array([group_fraction(0.5, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(0.5, 30, 25, rng)
                     for _ in range(200)])
    p = (null >= obs).mean() if obs > 0 else (null <= obs).mean()   # direction chosen after looking
    flagged += p < 0.05
print(f"accident rate with direction-after-looking: {flagged/2000:.3f}  (honest target: 0.05)")
```

With perfectly continuous measurements the rate is exactly double; the discreteness of counts
spares a little of it here. Nothing in any single computation looks wrong; the model of the
*procedure* is what's wrong —
the analysis answered a question shaped by the answer. The general form of this failure (chosen
thresholds, chosen subgroups, chosen outcomes — all chosen after looking) is among the most
common ways honest people produce false discoveries.

**The 1,200 questions are not 1,200 independent questions.** Neighboring CpG sites travel
together — methylation comes in coordinated regions, just as neighboring positions on a
chromosome are inherited together (geneticists call that *linkage*). Our null drew every site
independently. Correlated sites don't change any single p-value, but they change what a *list*
means: a run of ten significant neighbors may be one biological event wearing ten hats, and the
accident count fluctuates far more than independent-world arithmetic expects. When your
discoveries arrive in clumps, count events, not tests, before celebrating.

**And the null's own noise model can be too small for reality.** We built "nothing going on" as:
same true fraction, read-sampling wobble only. Real samples wobble for more reasons than reads —
sample handling, cell composition, day effects — so the real null world is *wider* than the one
we simulated, and every accident count above is a floor, not a promise. What happens when the
truth itself varies under the null — and how badly it breaks a scan exactly like this one — is
the entire subject of the next chapter (@sec-nest).

## Practice problems

Ungraded, solutions worked. Do them before looking.

### 2.1 · Predict the output {#sec-rep-p1}

A null scan of **5,000** sites, same settings as the chapter. Before running anything: what
shape is the p-value histogram, how many sites land below p = 0.01, and below p = 0.05?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Flat; about **50** below 0.01; about **250** below 0.05. No simulation needed — under the null,
p-values are uniform, so the count below $\alpha$ is $5000\alpha$ in expectation. If your scan of
real data shows a flat histogram with a spike near zero, the spike's *excess over flat* is your
first estimate of how much true signal exists — a trick worth remembering.
:::

### 2.2 · Modify the story {#sec-rep-2}

Rebuild the graded-list experiment with **90 samples per group** instead of 30. Before running:
which numbers in the list composition change, in which direction — and which number provably
does not move?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Power rises: group means tighten threefold in variance, so the 0.07 shifts stand out further and
essentially all 60 true sites are caught. The false-positive count **does not move**: truly-null
sites produce p < 0.05 five percent of the time at *any* sample size — bigger samples make real
effects easier to see, not accidents rarer. So the list grows more honest (60-ish real against
~57 accidents) but the accidents never leave. The only levers on the false count are the
threshold and the number of null questions asked.
:::

### 2.3 · Hand-calculate {#sec-rep-p3}

Five honest tests, all null, threshold 0.05. By hand: the probability that *at least one* comes
up significant. Then: the expected number that do.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Each test stays quiet with probability 0.95; all five stay quiet with $0.95^5 \approx 0.774$; so
at least one fires with probability $1 - 0.774 = \mathbf{0.226}$ — nearly a coin flip's worth of
risk from just five questions. Expected count: $5 \times 0.05 = 0.25$. Both numbers come from the
same two facts, multiplied — no simulation, no software, and they scale in your head: at 100
tests, "at least one" is a near-certainty ($1 - 0.95^{100} \approx 0.994$).
:::

### 2.4 · Spot the mismatch {#sec-rep-p4}

A paper reports: *"Of 12,000 genes tested, 640 reached p < 0.05. Since chance predicts 600, we
identified 40 genes whose expression truly changed."* The arithmetic is right. What is wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The subtraction lives at the level of *counts*; the claim lives at the level of *genes* — and
nothing connects them. An excess of 40 over the expected 600 is (weak) evidence that some signal
exists somewhere, but the 640 names on the list are ~600 accidents and ~40 truths *thoroughly
shuffled together*, and the analysis contains nothing that says which are which. "We identified
40 genes" asserts an identification that was never performed. The honest sentence: "the excess
suggests on the order of 40 real changes; individually, no gene on this list is more than about
6% likely to be one of them without further evidence."
:::

### 2.5 · Read the notation {#sec-rep-p5}

Translate $\mathbb{E}[\text{FP}] = m_{\text{null}}\,\alpha$ into one line of code for a 20,000-gene
scan at $\alpha = 0.01$, and one sentence for a collaborator deciding whether to trust a
180-gene discovery list from that scan.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
```{python}
print(20000 * 0.01)
```
Sentence: "even if *nothing* in your experiment changed, this scan hands you about 200 genes at
p < 0.01 — so a 180-gene list is not evidence of anything yet; it is *fewer* discoveries than
nothing-at-all typically produces, and the list needs a different threshold or a different
design before anyone spends money on it."
:::
